title: Visual constraints upon avian behaviour
why: A Cardiff PhD thesis on how avian behaviour is constrained by eye design: eye size, retinal image brightness and retinal topography compared across bird species (harvest abstract). The harvest listed it first of seven for "Pooecetes visual acuity" and second for "Pooecetes visual field"; OpenAlex search can match words in the full text, so a vesper sparrow may be named in its species comparisons, and the abstract start in the harvest names no species. Audit 46 read the ORCA record page (the author is Alexandra Louise Pollard) and found that the full abstract names only the European robin and Archaeopteryx, so a vesper sparrow is a long shot. Green open copy; not opened by this desk. The oa job's lookup by title found no open location (sources/oa-none-12); the harvest listing carries the Cardiff ORCA address. For Oriolus the harvest listed it first of 11 for "Oriolus visual acuity" and first of 340 for "Oriolus visual field", and the screen tool lists it as the one candidate for acuity_cpd and interreceptor_deg (words: eye size, retina). Its comparisons of eye size and retinal topography across species may name Oriolus oriolus, O. chinensis or O. sagittatus, though the abstract start names none. Not opened by this desk. [On main: also wanted by harvest-28.]
get: http://orca.cf.ac.uk/55002/1/U585391.pdf (green open copy from the harvest listing)

title: The role of the triommatidium in the visual behavior of apterous Aphis fabae Scop.
why: An open PhD thesis on the three-ommatidium eye of apterous Aphis fabae, a congener of the queue's Aphis nerii (optics carry within a genus). It came back for both acuity searches. Main holds one record from it (sweep-27, marked partial because it was read through a summariser): a 3 to 4 degree optomotor threshold with about 16 ommatidia per eye in first-instar nymphs rising to about 78 in adults; the record's note says the thesis gave no interommatidial angle or flicker value for A. fabae. A full read can confirm that, or find an angle between the ommatidial axes. Not opened by this desk. [On main: main holds 1 evidence record from it (sweep-27).]
get: https://theses.ncl.ac.uk/jspui/bitstream/10443/3621/1/Hum%2C%20M%201977.pdf (open PDF from the Newcastle theses repository)

title: UV sensitive vision in cardinals and tanagers is ubiquitous
why: Partial SWS1 opsin sequences from a broad sample of Cardinalidae and Thraupidae, all of the UV-sensitive type according to the abstract that earlier sweeps read.
